29.title: The sun for breakfast
29.hook: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, thinking it a mango; Indra's thunderbolt
29.howItsDone: Hanuman is one of the most widely worshipped figures in Hinduism; many Hindus visit his temples on Tuesdays or Saturdays, and his childhood stories are told to children as the start of his life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prasad, the offering that comes back, and a full week with Ganesha. This week belongs to another beloved god, and he starts out hungry.

A baby wakes up hungry. His mother is off gathering fruit. Low on the horizon he sees the rising sun, round and orange-red, exactly like a ripe mango. So he jumps for it. Not a hop: this baby is the son of the wind, and he shoots straight up into the sky, mouth open, reaching for breakfast. The gods watch in alarm. And Indra, king of the gods, lord of storms, does what a nervous king does. He throws his thunderbolt. It strikes the baby on the jaw, and he falls all the way to earth.
screen: `A HUNGRY BABY.` → `THE SUN LOOKS LIKE A MANGO.` → `HE LEAPS.` → `INDRA'S THUNDERBOLT.`

segments.voice: The baby is Hanuman, and the fall gives him his name. Hanu means jaw in Sanskrit. Hanuman: the one with the jaw, the one who was struck. The story is in the Ramayana, the great epic credited to the poet Valmiki, and it's told twice: an old bear, Jambavan, tells it to Hanuman himself, and a later book tells it again. Some tellings say a fruit; many families say a mango. Then comes a shape you've met before. Hanuman's father is Vayu, the wind. When his son falls, Vayu carries him into a cave and stops blowing. The whole world begins to suffocate. Like Parvati's grief on day twenty-three, a parent's grief brings everything to a halt. So the gods come, all of them. They heal the child, and each one gives him a gift: strength, speed, protection from weapons, a long life. Even Indra gives one. The baby knocked out of the sky goes home with more power than anyone. Look at the shape of it. Of course the reach was too big; you can't eat the sun. But the tradition doesn't mock him for it. It names him after it. The same wanting that sent him too high will one day carry him across an ocean. Reach anyway. You might fall. You might come home with gifts.
screen: `HANU — THE JAW.` · `TOLD IN THE RAMAYANA.` · `THE WIND STOPS.` · `EVERY GOD GIVES HIM A GIFT.` · then, large: `REACH ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly, like the wind coming back. Bring to mind something you want that feels far too big, a hope you'd hardly say out loud. Don't shrink it or argue with it; let it glow there, like the sun on the horizon.
Hanuman. The one with the jaw, named for the thunderbolt that struck him as he leapt for the sun.
Your line: reach anyway. Tomorrow, the strength he forgot he ever had. That's day twenty-nine.

30.title: The forgotten strength
30.hook: cursed to forget his powers until reminded
30.howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn traditionally credited to the poet Tulsidas, for courage in hard times; it retells Hanuman's deeds, including the crossing of the ocean.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman, the baby who leapt for the sun and came home with a gift from every god. Reach anyway.

A child with the strength of the wind, and no sense of limits, runs wild through the forest hermitages. Young Hanuman knocks over the sages' water pots and ritual vessels. He tears their bark clothes. Not cruel; just a kid who doesn't know his own size. The sages, patient people, reach the end of their patience. They don't take his strength away. They do something stranger. They curse him to forget it: all that power, and no memory of it, until someone reminds him.
screen: `A CHILD WITH NO LIMITS.` → `THE SAGES' PATIENCE ENDS.` → `HE WILL FORGET.` → `UNTIL SOMEONE REMINDS HIM.`

segments.voice: Years pass. Hanuman grows up gentle, wise and loyal, with no idea what he can do. Now jump ahead in the Ramayana. Monkeys and bears stand on the southern shore, staring at the ocean. Somewhere across it is the island of Lanka, a hundred yojanas away, the text says: an enormous distance. One by one the heroes say how far they could jump. Ten. Twenty. Fifty. Jambavan, the old bear, says ninety, now that he's old. Prince Angada could make the hundred, but isn't sure he could make it back. Nobody can do it. Hanuman sits apart, quiet. He doesn't even volunteer. Then Jambavan walks over and tells Hanuman his own story. You are the son of the wind. As a baby you leapt for the sun. Every god gave you a gift. Why are you sitting here silent? As he speaks, Hanuman remembers. The text says he begins to grow, in size and strength, until the others cheer. So the strength was never gone. It was forgotten. That's a different problem: forgetting what you've already survived, already done, already are. And the curse isn't lifted by a god. It's lifted by a friend who remembers you better than you remember yourself, and tells you your own story back.

segments.voice: Sit, breathe, and be your own Jambavan for a minute. Recall a hard thing you got through, or a time you were braver than you expected. Tell yourself plainly, the way the old bear did: you did this. Then let it grow a little.
Jambavan. The old bear at the ocean's edge who reminds Hanuman of the strength he forgot.
Your line: you're stronger than you remember. Tomorrow, a meeting in disguise. Day thirty, done.

31.title: Meeting Rama
31.hook: the disguised monkey meets the exiled prince
31.howItsDone: Hanuman is honored as the model devotee of Rama; in temples his image often kneels or stands before Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, and devotees chant Rama's name in his honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jambavan, the old bear who told Hanuman his own story back. You're stronger than you remember.

A monkey king is hiding on a forest mountain. Sugriva has been driven from his kingdom by his own brother, and he's scared of everyone. Then two men come walking up the valley: tall, dressed like hermits in bark, but carrying bows. Assassins, he thinks, sent by his brother. So he sends his most trusted adviser to find out. Hanuman. And Hanuman goes in disguise too, as a wandering holy man. He bows to the strangers and asks polite, careful questions. Two sides, both hiding who they are, trying to read each other.
screen: `A KING IN HIDING.` → `TWO ARMED HERMITS.` → `HANUMAN IN DISGUISE.`

segments.voice: The two men are Rama, a prince in exile, and his brother Lakshmana. Rama's wife, Sita, has been taken; you'll hear the whole story from its start in a few days. Watch what happens when Hanuman speaks. In Valmiki's Ramayana, Rama turns to his brother and says, more or less: listen to him. Nobody talks like this without deep study. Not one word out of place, not too long, not too rushed, every sentence clear and kind. Someone who speaks like this could win over an enemy with a raised sword. Rama knows Hanuman by how he talks, before he knows who he is. And Hanuman knows Rama. He drops the disguise, shows his true form, lifts both brothers onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to his king. Later tellings go further. In the Ramcharitmanas, the poet Tulsidas's retelling, Hanuman falls at Rama's feet the moment he knows him. In devotional tradition, this is where his heart shows: from here on, his life is devotion to Rama. That's bhakti, your sixteenth word, with a face. Neither knew the other by clothes; both were in disguise. Each knew the other by how he spoke, what he noticed, how he treated a stranger. You know your people. And when Hanuman finds his, he carries them home.

Meeting Rama. Two disguises, and each knows the other by how he speaks.
Your line: you know your people, by how they speak and what they notice. See you tomorrow.

32.title: The leap
32.hook: the ocean to Lanka; Surasa's mouth; the mountain that offers rest
32.howItsDone: Some Hindus read or recite the Sundara Kanda, the Ramayana's book of Hanuman's journey, as a devotional practice, sometimes in full over a day or across several days, especially in difficult times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: meeting Rama. Two disguises, and a prince known by how he speaks. You know your people.

Hanuman climbs a mountain on the shore and grows huge. He presses down so hard that the rocks crack and the trees shake loose their flowers. Then he jumps. The text makes a spectacle of it: blossoms pulled along behind him, his shadow racing over the waves like a ship. He's flying to Lanka to find Sita. Halfway across, a mountain named Mainaka rises out of the sea, and speaks. You're doing a great thing for a good cause. Rest on me. Eat some fruit. A kind offer, from a real mountain, right there.
screen: `HE CRACKS THE MOUNTAIN.` → `HE JUMPS.` → `A MOUNTAIN RISES: REST ON ME.`

segments.voice: Hanuman thanks the mountain. He touches it politely with his hand and says: I've made a promise; I can't stop. And he flies on. That's the first test: a good thing that would slow you down. The second comes straight after. The gods send Surasa, mother of serpents, to see what he's made of. She rises from the water, mouth open: nobody passes me without going in. Hanuman grows bigger. She opens wider. Bigger. Wider. It could go on forever. Then he does the clever thing. He shrinks to the size of a thumb, darts into her mouth and straight back out, and bows. I went in. Now let me go. Surasa laughs and blesses him. Second test: not everything is won by getting bigger. A third follows, Simhika, a creature who grabs shadows, and he defeats her too. All of this is in the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book, the fifth book of Valmiki's Ramayana. It's Hanuman's book, and some Hindus recite it whole, as a devotion, in hard times. So the leap isn't one jump. It's a string of small choices in midair: decline the comfortable rest, skip the size contest, keep going. The leap is the practice.
screen: `THANK THE MOUNTAIN. FLY ON.` · `SURASA'S MOUTH.` · `GET SMALL AND QUICK.` · `THE SUNDARA KANDA.` · then, large: `THE LEAP IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Name one thing you keep meaning to start: a call, a class, a hard conversation. Picture the mountain offering rest, later, not today, and thank it kindly, the way Hanuman did. Then picture just the first moment of the leap.
The leap. The ocean to Lanka: a mountain declined, and Surasa outwitted by getting small.
Your line: the leap is the practice, one small choice after another. That's thirty-two days.

33.title: Finding Sita
33.hook: the garden; the ring; "I'm not leaving without you"
33.howItsDone: The scene of Hanuman giving Rama's ring to Sita in the ashoka grove is often painted and performed, and it's a high point when devotees recite the Sundara Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the leap. A mountain thanked and passed, and a thumb-sized escape from Surasa's mouth.

Lanka at night: a city of gold, full of music, feasting and guards. Hanuman shrinks to the size of a cat and searches, palace after palace, room after room. He sees the demon king Ravana's wives asleep, and for a moment wonders if one is Sita. Then he stops himself. No. Sita would never sleep peacefully here. He almost gives up. Then, at the city's edge, a grove of ashoka trees. Under one tree, guarded by fierce women, sits a woman in a single worn cloth, thin from grief, refusing everything she's offered. He climbs into the branches above her and waits.
screen: `A CITY OF GOLD, AT NIGHT.` → `NOT HER. NOT HERE.` → `A GARDEN OF ASHOKA TREES.` → `A WOMAN UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman has a problem. If a giant monkey drops out of a tree in the enemy's city and says Rama sent me, she'll scream, and he'll be caught. So he does something gentle. Hidden in the leaves, he softly tells Rama's story, the one she knows best. Sita looks up. He comes down, bows, and gives her the one proof of who he is: Rama's ring. She holds it, the text says, with joy, as though she'd found her husband again. Then Hanuman offers: climb on my back, and I'll carry you across the ocean tonight. It's easy to remember this as Hanuman saying, I'm not leaving without you. But in Valmiki, the one who says no is Sita. She gives two reasons. She won't willingly touch any man but her husband. And she wants Rama to come himself and end this properly. She takes a jewel from her hair for Hanuman, and tells him a small private story only Rama would know, so Rama will believe him. Ring in, jewel out. Weigh what crossed the ocean: something tiny, proof she wasn't forgotten. In a city full of voices telling her to give up, that ring said someone is coming. Bring the ring. Whoever is waiting needs proof you remember.
screen: `HE TELLS RAMA'S STORY, SOFTLY.` · `THE RING.` · `CLIMB ON MY BACK. SHE SAYS NO.` · `RING IN, JEWEL OUT.` · then, large: `BRING THE RING.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Hold in mind someone who is waiting on you, even if they never say so: a parent, a friend going through something, a child. Keep them with you for the whole sit. If you pray, hold them before God.
Finding Sita. In the ashoka grove: Rama's ring in, her hair jewel out.
Your line: bring the ring. Small, real proof that someone isn't forgotten. Day thirty-three, done.

34.title: The burning tail
34.hook: caught, set on fire, burns Lanka with it
34.howItsDone: The burning of Lanka is a favorite scene in Ramlila performances across North India, and devotees recite it as part of the Sundara Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a ring in, a jewel out, and Sita's quiet no. Bring the ring.

The job is done. He's found Sita and has her jewel. He could slip away tonight and no one in Lanka would know. Instead, Hanuman wants to see the enemy up close, so he does something loud. He tears up the royal garden, tree by tree, and fights off wave after wave of warriors. Finally Ravana's son, Indrajit, binds him with a divine weapon. Hanuman could break free. He lets himself be dragged into the court of the ten-headed king. He wanted to be caught: it was the only way in the front door.
screen: `THE JOB IS DONE.` → `HE TEARS UP THE GARDEN.` → `HE LETS THEM CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: Before Ravana, Hanuman speaks plainly: give Sita back, make peace with Rama. Ravana, furious, orders him killed. His younger brother, Vibhishana, objects: you don't kill a messenger; that's not how kings behave. Remember Vibhishana; he matters later. So Ravana picks a humiliation instead. A monkey's pride is his tail, he says. Burn it. The guards wrap the tail in rags, soak it in oil, set it alight, and parade Hanuman through the streets to laughter. Then he shrinks, slips his ropes, grows huge again and leaps onto the rooftops. Tail blazing, he jumps from palace to palace, and the golden city goes up in flames. The text adds something tender. When Sita hears they've set his tail on fire, she prays to Agni, god of fire, that it be cool for him. Mid-leap, Hanuman notices the fire isn't hurting him at all. Then panic: what if I've burned the garden where she is? He rushes back. She's safe. The fire went everywhere but to her. Notice who picked the weapon. Ravana chose the fire, to make a fool of him. Hanuman turned it into a message. Sometimes the setback, the insult, the thing meant to shrink you, is exactly the tool you needed. Use what they hand you.

Lanka. Ravana's golden island city, set ablaze by the tail they lit to shame Hanuman.
Your line: use what they hand you, even the fire meant to shame you. That's day thirty-four.

35.title: The mountain of herbs
35.hook: can't remember which herb — brings the mountain
35.howItsDone: Many Hindus call on Hanuman as Sankat Mochan in times of trouble, visiting his temples, including the Sankat Mochan temple in Varanasi, and reciting the Hanuman Chalisa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lanka ablaze, the burning tail, and a humiliation turned into a message. Your line was use what they hand you. Today ends Hanuman's week, with a picture of him you may have seen: a monkey flying, holding a mountain. Day thirty-five.

Jump ahead, to the war for Lanka. Night on the battlefield. Rama's brother Lakshmana lies struck down by a terrible weapon, barely breathing. The healer in the camp says there's one hope: certain herbs that grow on a mountain in the Himalayas, far to the north. Bring them before sunrise, and he lives. It's a vast distance. Only one of them could cover it that fast. Hanuman goes. He crosses the land in the dark, finds the mountain, lands. And he stops. There are plants everywhere, glowing in the night. He doesn't know which ones are the herbs. And the sun will not wait.

So he picks up the whole mountain. Tears the peak off, balances it on one hand, and flies it back to the battlefield. The healer finds the herbs, and Lakshmana lives. That image, Hanuman in the sky with a mountain on his palm, turns up on calendars, temple walls and truck doors. Valmiki's Ramayana tells the herb-mountain journey in its war book, more than once, and later tellings, like the race against sunrise, add their own details. Today's word comes from this Hanuman. Sankat mochan. Sankat means trouble, a crisis, a tight spot. Mochan means release, setting free. The one who frees you from trouble. It's a name people call him by. In Varanasi there's a great temple by that name, and people who are frightened, sick, broke or grieving go and stand before him. Look at the choice he made. When he didn't know exactly what was needed, he didn't wait until he did. He brought everything. That's seva, your fifteenth word, at full size: service that doesn't do the minimum. Now look back at the week. A baby who reached for the sun. A strength forgotten, and a friend who remembered. A meeting where two disguises fell away. A leap made of small choices. A ring carried across an ocean. A fire turned into a message. And a whole mountain, because one leaf might have been the wrong one. Tomorrow, the Ramayana begins, from the very start.
screen: `HE LIFTS THE WHOLE PEAK.` · `SANKAT MOCHAN — FREER FROM TROUBLE.` · `SEVA AT FULL SIZE.` · `A WEEK WITH HANUMAN.` · then, large: `BRING THE WHOLE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a seva review. Sit and breathe. Look back over the last week. Where did you serve someone? A favor, a meal, time, attention. Where did you do the minimum when you could have brought more? No guilt; this isn't a scoreboard. Just notice. Then think of one person in trouble right now, and ask: what would bringing the whole mountain look like, for them, this week? The bell holds the time.
Sankat mochan. The one who frees from trouble: Hanuman, who flew a mountain through the night so a friend would live.
Your line: bring the whole mountain. Today, for one person in trouble, don't do the minimum. Day thirty-five.

fork.setup: you're Hanuman on a mountain at night. you need one herb before sunrise, and you can't tell which it is. what do you do?
options: search leaf by leaf and hope.
fly back and ask the healer to describe it again.
lift the whole mountain and carry it back.
fork.reveal: he brings the entire peak. the healer finds the herbs, and Lakshmana lives.

original.note: Hindi, from Sanskrit: the one who frees (mochana) from trouble (sankata).

trapdoor: what you thought: a strongman picture of a monkey holding a rock.
what it means: when he didn't know exactly what was needed, he brought everything. sankat mochan, the freer from trouble.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki's war book tells the herb-mountain journey more than once, Lakshmana's wound among them; later tellings, including Tulsidas, add their own details.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Hanuman brings the herb mountain)
Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kanda (Lakshmana struck; Hanuman brings the mountain)
